Day 49 of 100 · Linux Administration

SSH Deep Dive

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished artifact recovered

SSH combines remote access, key authentication and host verification, but small permission or trust mistakes can make secure access fail or become unsafe.

Architecture / mental model

SSH client → host-key verification + authentication negotiation → sshd → remote session

How it works

SSH first needs to establish that the server identity is acceptable to the client, then negotiate an authentication method for the user. Host keys and user keys solve different trust questions.

Key-based authentication avoids repeatedly sending a reusable password to each remote host. An Ed25519 key can be generated with `ssh-keygen` and the public key installed for the intended account.

Verbose client output is one of the fastest ways to understand failed authentication because it shows configuration, candidate keys and methods the client is actually trying.

Hands-on reference

ssh user@server_ip
ssh -p 2222 user@server_ip
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user@server_ip
ssh -v user@server_ip
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'admin@laptop'

Verification

Connect with verbose output in a lab, confirm the expected host key and authentication key are used, then remove or disable an obsolete credential and prove it no longer works.

Field note / gotcha

Private-key and `.ssh` permissions can cause OpenSSH to reject keys. Another dangerous shortcut is bypassing host-key verification instead of understanding why the server identity changed.

Security considerations

Protect private keys with filesystem permissions and passphrases where appropriate, disable unnecessary password/root login, and keep host-key verification enabled.

What I learned

Remote access is two trust decisions: is this the server I intended, and am I an identity this server should authorize?
